scenario: An engineer wants a supervisory script that flags any completed session whose last recorded response has a stop_reason other than a clean finish, so a human can review incomplete or truncated runs.
stem: Which stop_reason values should the script treat as needing review rather than a clean completion?

options.text: Only "max_tokens", since that's the only value indicating the response was cut off.
Both "tool_use" and "max_tokens" — a final stored response with "tool_use" means the loop stopped before executing an outstanding request, and "max_tokens" means generation was cut short.
"end_turn" only, since it is the value most often confused with a genuine completion.
None of them — a script should trust the presence of a final assistant message alone, regardless of stop_reason.

rationale.correct: A stored final response with stop_reason: "tool_use" means the loop stopped without ever executing (or continuing past) a pending tool call — a sign the process was interrupted or crashed, not that it finished cleanly. "max_tokens" means the response was truncated mid-generation. Both are legitimate review triggers; "end_turn" (and a configured "stop_sequence") represent the model choosing to stop on its own terms and don't need review.

distractors.A: max_tokens alone misses the tool_use case, which is an equally strong signal that the run didn't finish as intended.
distractors.C: end_turn is exactly the normal, clean completion signal the script should NOT flag — flagging it would generate constant false alarms.
distractors.D: The presence of a final assistant message says nothing about whether the run actually completed; stop_reason is the field that distinguishes a clean finish from a truncated or interrupted one.

scenario: Your loop's next request must include the assistant's prior response. That prior response contained both an explanatory text block ('Let me check the current inventory level.') and a `tool_use` block requesting `check_inventory`.
stem: How should the assistant turn be constructed in the next request's message history?

options.text: Include the entire prior assistant message exactly as returned — both the text block and the tool_use block — so the model's own reasoning and its tool request stay together in context.
Include only the tool_use block; discard the text block since it isn't needed once the tool has been executed.
Include only the text block; the tool_use block is redundant once the tool_result is appended.
Merge the text and tool_use content into a single flattened string before appending.

rationale.correct: An assistant turn can contain multiple content blocks of different types in one message. The full message — text and tool_use together — must be preserved and appended as-is; the model's own prior turn is not something the loop edits or trims.

distractors.B: Discarding the text block removes context (the model's stated reasoning) that may matter for later turns, and there's no reason the loop needs to edit the assistant's own prior message.
distractors.C: Discarding the tool_use block breaks the pairing tool_result blocks rely on (they're matched to a specific tool_use by ID), corrupting the next request.
distractors.D: Flattening structured content blocks into a string discards the API's content-block structure, which the next request needs intact to correctly pair tool_use with its tool_result.

scenario: A developer new to the Claude API writes a loop that checks `response.tool_calls` to decide whether to execute tools, based on patterns they've used with other providers' APIs.
stem: What is wrong with this check?

options.text: The Claude API has no `tool_calls` field; tool requests appear as `content` blocks with `type: "tool_use"`, and the presence of tool_use content combined with `stop_reason: "tool_use"` is what the loop should check instead.
Nothing is wrong; `tool_calls` is simply an older, deprecated name for the same field.
The check is correct, but it should also inspect `stop_reason` in addition, not instead.
`tool_calls` is correct, but it only appears when `tool_choice` is set to `"any"`.

rationale.correct: This is a common carryover mistake from other providers' APIs. Claude's response represents tool requests as content blocks of type `tool_use` inside the `content` array, signaled by `stop_reason: "tool_use"` — there is no top-level `tool_calls` field to check.

distractors.B: There's no deprecated `tool_calls` field in the Claude API at any point — this isn't a naming migration, it's checking a field that doesn't exist.
distractors.C: This assumes `tool_calls` exists and just needs a companion check; the actual fix is checking the correct fields entirely (content blocks and stop_reason), not adding to a nonexistent one.
distractors.D: `tool_choice` controls which tool(s) the model is permitted/forced to call; it has no bearing on what field name the response uses to represent tool requests.

scenario: Your loop's stop-condition check only branches on two values: continue on `"tool_use"`, return the response on `"end_turn"`. In production, a request occasionally comes back with `stop_reason: "stop_sequence"` because a custom stop sequence you configured was matched, and your loop currently falls through with no matching branch and crashes.
stem: How should the loop handle `"stop_sequence"`?

options.text: Treat it as another valid terminal state — like `"end_turn"` — and return the response, since the model stopped deliberately at a configured boundary rather than being cut off or requesting a tool.
Treat it identically to `"tool_use"` and attempt to execute a tool, since any non-`"end_turn"` value implies more work remains.
Treat it as an error condition and retry the request unchanged.
Ignore `stop_reason` entirely going forward and just check whether the response contains any tool_use blocks.

rationale.correct: `"stop_sequence"` is a legitimate terminal stop_reason meaning generation stopped at a custom sequence you configured — it's not an error and not a tool request. The loop's stop-condition logic needs to recognize the full set of terminal states, not just `"end_turn"`.

distractors.B: There's no tool_use content to execute here; treating a terminal state as a tool request would look for tool_use blocks that don't exist.
distractors.C: This isn't an error — retrying an already-successful request that matched its stop sequence doesn't address the actual gap, which is a missing branch in the stop-condition logic.
distractors.D: Dropping `stop_reason` and inferring from content presence alone is exactly the anti-pattern the loop's design is meant to avoid; the fix is adding the missing terminal-state branch, not abandoning the structured signal.

scenario: A coordinator agent is supposed to delegate to search, document-analysis, synthesis, and report subagents, but it never delegates — it attempts every step itself.
stem: What is the most likely configuration problem?

options.text: The coordinator's allowedTools does not include "Task."
The subagents are missing system prompts.
tool_choice is set to "any."
The coordinator's max_tokens is too low to delegate.

rationale.correct: Subagents are spawned via the Task tool, so the coordinator can only invoke them if its allowedTools includes "Task"; without it, the coordinator has no way to delegate at all.

distractors.B: Missing subagent system prompts would affect subagent quality once invoked, not whether the coordinator can spawn them in the first place.
distractors.C: tool_choice governs whether/which tool must be called on a given turn; it doesn't control which tools are available.
distractors.D: max_tokens limits output length and doesn't govern the ability to invoke a tool.

scenario: A coordinator's iterative refinement loop has already run three re-delegation rounds on a market-research report, and each round still finds a subtopic that could be slightly deeper.
stem: What should determine when the coordinator stops iterating rather than continuing indefinitely?

options.text: Always run exactly one refinement round regardless of the findings, to bound cost.
Continue until every subtopic is exhaustively covered, since more depth is always better for a research report.
Stop once remaining gaps fall below a defined sufficiency bar (e.g., minor detail rather than a missing subtopic), balancing coverage against diminishing returns.
Never re-delegate more than once per subtopic, regardless of how thin the resulting coverage is.

rationale.correct: Iterative refinement should continue only while it is closing meaningful gaps; once remaining gaps are minor rather than substantive, further rounds cost more than they add. A defined sufficiency bar keeps the loop from running indefinitely on marginal improvements.

distractors.A: A fixed one-round rule ignores whether that round actually closed the gaps; some reports need more, others need none.
distractors.B: Exhaustive coverage has no natural stopping point and would make the loop run indefinitely at unbounded cost.
distractors.D: Capping re-delegation at one attempt per subtopic regardless of outcome can leave a real gap unresolved even when one more targeted pass would close it.

scenario: A coordinator's system prompt is 3,000 words long, containing detailed domain knowledge about tax law, refund policy edge cases, and product specifications — the same material already duplicated across each subagent's own system prompt.
stem: What is the most maintainable way to organize this?

options.text: Keep the coordinator's system prompt focused on orchestration — when to delegate, how to decide which subagents to invoke, and how to synthesize their outputs — and let each subagent's own system prompt own the domain expertise it actually needs.
Keep all domain knowledge duplicated in both places, since the coordinator might need it as a fallback if a subagent is unavailable.
Move all domain knowledge out of subagent prompts entirely and centralize it only in the coordinator's prompt, since subagents already receive delegated tasks.
Split the domain knowledge alphabetically between the coordinator and the subagents to balance prompt length.

rationale.correct: The coordinator's job is orchestration — routing, delegation, and synthesis — not doing the domain work itself. Domain expertise belongs in the subagent(s) that actually perform that work; duplicating it in the coordinator's prompt too just creates two places that can drift out of sync.

distractors.B: Deliberately duplicating content 'just in case' guarantees drift between the two copies over time and bloats the coordinator's prompt with knowledge it doesn't act on directly.
distractors.C: Subagents perform the actual domain work and need that expertise directly; stripping it from them and centralizing only in the coordinator misplaces the knowledge relative to where it's used.
distractors.D: An arbitrary split like alphabetical order has nothing to do with which agent actually needs which knowledge to do its job.

scenario: For a straightforward task — 'summarize this quarter's three sales reports' — a coordinator spawns nine subagents: one per report per aspect (revenue, trends, outliers), reasoning that finer-grained subagents will each produce cleaner output.
stem: What is the problem with this approach?

options.text: The task's actual complexity doesn't warrant nine subagents; the coordinator should scope subagent count to what the task needs, since over-spawning adds coordination and synthesis overhead without a proportional quality gain for a task this simple.
Nothing — more subagents always produce higher-quality results regardless of task complexity.
Nine subagents will exceed the Task tool's per-turn call limit and the request will fail outright.
The problem is exclusively that nine parallel Task calls will exceed rate limits; sequential invocation would fix it.

rationale.correct: Subagent count should match task complexity. Three simple, similar reports don't need nine narrowly-sliced subagents — that just adds nine outputs to reconcile and coordinate for no real quality benefit over a couple of well-scoped subagents (or even direct handling).

distractors.B: More subagents isn't automatically better; past the point where the task's actual structure calls for it, additional subagents mostly add coordination overhead and redundant partial results to reconcile.
distractors.C: There's no fixed universal per-turn call limit at play here — the real problem is task/subagent-count mismatch, not a hard technical ceiling.
distractors.D: Rate limits are an infrastructure concern, not the core design issue; the point is that nine subagents is disproportionate to three simple reports regardless of how the calls are batched.

scenario: Your system has three registered subagent types: `web-researcher` (broad web search), `document-analyzer` (structured extraction from provided documents), and `fact-checker` (narrow, single-claim verification). The coordinator receives a request to verify one specific statistic against an already-provided report.
stem: Which subagent type should the coordinator invoke, and why?

options.text: `fact-checker`, because the task is a narrow, single-claim verification against material already on hand, not open-ended research or general document extraction.
`web-researcher`, because verification tasks should always default to the broadest-capability subagent available.
`document-analyzer`, because any task involving a report should go to the subagent whose name mentions documents, regardless of the specific task.
All three, in parallel, so their outputs can be cross-checked against each other.

rationale.correct: Matching the task's actual shape — a narrow, single-claim check against material already provided — to the subagent type built for exactly that (`fact-checker`) is more precise and efficient than defaulting to a broader-capability agent or picking by superficial name association.

distractors.B: Defaulting to the broadest subagent regardless of task shape wastes capability and doesn't reflect how subagent types should be selected.
distractors.C: Picking by keyword match on the subagent's name rather than the actual task ignores what each type is actually built to do.
distractors.D: Invoking all three in parallel for a single simple verification is wasteful; the task doesn't call for multiple perspectives, just one targeted check.

scenario: A coordinator needs a synthesis subagent to combine findings, but synthesis can only meaningfully begin once the search and document-analysis subagents have both completed their work on the same topic.
stem: How should the coordinator sequence these three subagent invocations?

options.text: Spawn search and document-analysis in parallel (since they're independent of each other), then spawn synthesis afterward, once both have returned results to pass into its prompt.
Spawn all three in parallel in a single response, since parallel spawning always minimizes latency regardless of task dependencies.
Spawn them one at a time in an arbitrary order, since Task tool calls must always run sequentially.
Spawn synthesis first so it's ready to receive results as they arrive.

rationale.correct: Parallelizing only applies to genuinely independent work; search and document-analysis don't depend on each other, so they can run in parallel, but synthesis depends on both of their outputs and must wait until it has real content to synthesize.

distractors.B: Parallel spawning helps only when the spawned tasks are actually independent; spawning synthesis before its inputs exist wastes the call since it would have nothing to synthesize.
distractors.C: Task tool calls are not required to run strictly sequentially — independent ones can and should be parallelized; the constraint here is data dependency, not a blanket sequencing rule.
distractors.D: Spawning synthesis before its dependencies have produced anything gives it no findings to work with.

scenario: You need to analyze five different vendor contracts for the same three risk factors. A single `contract-analyzer` subagent type is registered.
stem: How should the coordinator use this one subagent type to analyze all five contracts?

options.text: Spawn five separate invocations of the same `contract-analyzer` subagent type in parallel, one per contract, since the type doesn't limit how many times or how often it can be instantiated.
Register five new subagent types, one per contract, since each invocation requires its own distinct type.
Invoke `contract-analyzer` once with all five contracts concatenated into a single prompt.
Invoke `contract-analyzer` once, then manually copy its output four more times for the remaining contracts.

rationale.correct: A subagent type is a reusable template, not a one-time-use resource — it can be instantiated as many times as needed, including multiple parallel instances of the same type each working on a different input. Five parallel invocations, one per contract, correctly isolates each analysis while reusing the one registered type.

distractors.B: Registering a new type per contract confuses 'type' (a reusable role definition) with 'instance' (a specific invocation) — the existing type already generalizes across any contract.
distractors.C: Concatenating five contracts into one prompt loses the benefit of isolated per-document analysis and risks the model conflating details across contracts.
distractors.D: Copying one contract's analysis output for four unrelated contracts produces incorrect results for four of the five documents.

scenario: A coordinator spawns three parallel `document-analyzer` subagents, one per report, each with a prompt describing only what to look for. Each returns findings in its own ad hoc structure — one as prose paragraphs, one as a bulleted list, one as a table — and the synthesis subagent that consumes all three struggles to combine them consistently.
stem: What should be added to each subagent's invocation to fix this?

options.text: An explicit output-format specification (e.g., a required structure or schema each subagent's response must follow), so all three subagents return findings the synthesis subagent can process uniformly.
A request for each subagent to write in a more 'professional' tone.
A larger max_tokens budget for each subagent, so their outputs can be longer.
An instruction telling each subagent to guess what format the others are likely using.

rationale.correct: The problem is inconsistent output shape, not content quality — each subagent needs an explicit, shared format specification (fields, structure) in its invocation so their outputs are uniform and mechanically combinable by synthesis, rather than each inventing its own ad hoc structure.

distractors.B: Tone has nothing to do with structural inconsistency between prose, a bulleted list, and a table.
distractors.C: More tokens lets each subagent write more, not more consistently — it doesn't constrain the output shape at all.
distractors.D: Having each subagent guess at the others' format is unreliable and doesn't establish a real shared contract; an explicit specification given to all three does.

scenario: A support agent's prerequisite gate blocks process_refund until get_customer returns a verified ID. The team is now adding a new process_exchange tool that has the same identity-verification requirement.
stem: What is the most maintainable way to extend the enforcement to the new tool?

options.text: Duplicate the verification logic inline inside process_exchange's own handler, separately from process_refund's gate.
Extend the shared prerequisite-gate mechanism to also cover process_exchange, so both tools enforce the same identity check through one reusable rule.
Add a system-prompt reminder telling the agent to verify identity before using process_exchange.
Skip enforcement for process_exchange since it doesn't move money directly.

rationale.correct: A shared, reusable prerequisite-gate mechanism that any money- or identity-sensitive tool can register with keeps enforcement centralized and consistent, rather than re-implementing (and risking a slightly different, buggy version of) the same check per tool.

distractors.A: Duplicating the logic per tool creates multiple copies to keep in sync and is exactly the maintenance burden a shared mechanism avoids.
distractors.C: A prompt reminder is probabilistic, not deterministic, and doesn't meet the bar this exam guide sets for identity/financial enforcement.
distractors.D: Exchanges still touch customer identity and account state; skipping enforcement here reopens the same misidentification risk the gate was built to close.

scenario: Refund approval thresholds differ by customer tier: standard customers need approval above $500, while premium customers are approved automatically up to $2,000.
stem: How should this tiered threshold be enforced?

options.text: A single hard-coded $500 gate for everyone, with premium customers manually overridden case by case.
A programmatic gate that looks up the customer's tier and applies the corresponding threshold before allowing process_refund to proceed.
A system-prompt instruction listing both thresholds and asking the agent to apply the correct one.
Remove the gate entirely and rely on the agent's judgment about what "seems reasonable" per tier.

rationale.correct: The enforcement mechanism should stay programmatic and deterministic even when the rule has multiple cases; a gate that looks up tier and applies the matching threshold generalizes the same guarantee to tiered policy without falling back to probabilistic prompt compliance.

distractors.A: Manual overrides for premium customers reintroduce exactly the case-by-case inconsistency a gate is meant to eliminate.
distractors.C: A prompt listing both thresholds is still probabilistic compliance and can misapply the wrong threshold under the same failure modes as a single-threshold prompt.
distractors.D: Removing enforcement entirely abandons the guarantee altogether, worse than either prior option.

scenario: A support agent escalates and hands off a summary containing the customer ID, root cause, and refund amount, but no recommended action.
stem: What is the most likely consequence of omitting the recommended action, and what should be added?

options.text: No real consequence; a human agent with the other three fields can always infer the right next step unaided.
The receiving human must re-derive what the agent already concluded should happen, slowing resolution; the handoff should include a specific recommended action.
The omission is intentional best practice, since humans should always decide the action independently of the agent's assessment.
The fix is to include the full conversation transcript instead, so the human can read everything themselves.

rationale.correct: A structured handoff's purpose is to let the human act immediately without reconstructing context. Omitting the recommended action forces them to redo reasoning the agent already performed, defeating the point of a structured summary — the fix is to add it, not to compensate with unrelated fields.

distractors.A: The other three fields describe the situation but not what to do about it; assuming the human will infer the same conclusion the agent reached is not guaranteed and reintroduces delay.
distractors.C: A recommendation from the agent doesn't remove the human's authority to decide; it's a starting point that speeds resolution, not a bypass of judgment.
distractors.D: A full transcript is exactly the unstructured, slow-to-parse alternative a structured handoff exists to avoid.

scenario: A hook blocks a $1,200 refund (over the $500 auto-approval limit) and redirects the case to human escalation. The escalation queue currently just receives the generic message: 'Action blocked: refund exceeds policy limit.'
stem: What is missing from this redirect?

options.text: A structured handoff carrying the case's actual details — customer ID, requested amount, and reason for the original request — so the human reviewer can act without re-investigating from scratch.
Nothing; a generic message is sufficient since the human can look up the case themselves.
A retry loop that keeps re-attempting the refund at smaller amounts until one clears the limit.
A second hook that double-checks the first hook's decision before escalating.

rationale.correct: Enforcement and handoff are two halves of the same workflow: blocking the action deterministically is only half the job — the redirect needs to carry a structured handoff (the specific case facts) so the human receiving it can act immediately, the same way any escalation handoff should.

distractors.B: Forcing the human to look up the case from scratch defeats the purpose of an automated handoff and slows resolution.
distractors.C: Auto-retrying at smaller amounts attempts to route around the policy limit rather than correctly escalating a case that requires human approval.
distractors.D: A second redundant hook doesn't address the actual gap, which is the missing case context in the handoff itself.

scenario: A `process_refund` tool call is missing the `currency` parameter, which the model consistently omits even though your account only ever processes refunds in USD. Manually re-prompting the model each time to include it is unreliable.
stem: What is the most robust fix?

options.text: A PreToolUse hook that inspects the outgoing `process_refund` call and, if `currency` is absent, injects the default value "USD" before the call executes.
A system-prompt reminder telling the model to always include `currency`.
A PostToolUse hook that adds `currency` to the tool's result after it has already executed.
Reject any `process_refund` call missing `currency` and ask the model to retry from scratch.

rationale.correct: A PreToolUse hook runs before the call executes and can deterministically fill in a known, constant default the model keeps omitting — guaranteeing the parameter is present rather than relying on the model to remember it every time.

distractors.B: A prompt reminder is still probabilistic; that's exactly the unreliability already observed.
distractors.C: By the time PostToolUse runs, the call has already executed — possibly with the missing parameter already causing an error or wrong behavior. Adding it after the fact doesn't fix the call itself.
distractors.D: Rejecting and retrying wastes a full round trip for a gap that can be filled deterministically and silently before execution.

scenario: Company policy limits each customer to 2 refunds per rolling 24-hour period, regardless of amount. A single call's arguments never reveal how many refunds that customer has already received today.
stem: What must the enforcement hook do differently from a simple per-call limit check?

options.text: Maintain and consult persistent state (a count of recent refunds per customer) across calls, since this rule depends on the customer's refund history, not anything visible in a single call's arguments.
Nothing extra; a PreToolUse hook that only inspects the current call's arguments is sufficient, since the limit is enforced per call.
Increase the system prompt's emphasis on the 2-refund limit so the model tracks it itself.
Reject every second `process_refund` call unconditionally, regardless of which customer it is for.

rationale.correct: A per-customer, rolling-window limit is a cross-call rule: the hook needs to track and check state that persists across invocations (e.g., a per-customer counter with a timestamp), not just validate what's inside any single call's arguments.

distractors.B: A single call's arguments have no way of expressing how many refunds this customer already received today — that information doesn't exist without persistent state to consult.
distractors.C: Relying on the model to self-track a count across turns is exactly the kind of stateful bookkeeping a probabilistic instruction can't be trusted to enforce correctly every time.
distractors.D: Rejecting every second call regardless of customer breaks the rule entirely — the limit is per-customer, not a flat count across all customers.

scenario: Two PreToolUse hooks are both registered for `process_refund`: one verifies the customer's identity has been confirmed, and one checks the refund amount against the $500 limit. A refund with an unverified identity AND an amount of $800 comes through.
stem: What is the correct behavior?

options.text: Both conditions are real, independent violations, so the call should be blocked — it's sufficient that any registered PreToolUse hook for this tool call rejects it; which one reports first doesn't change the outcome of blocking the call.
Only the first-registered hook should run; the second is skipped once one hook exists.
The call should be allowed, since a call is only blocked if every registered hook rejects it.
The two hooks will conflict and the tool call will silently execute without any enforcement.

rationale.correct: Multiple PreToolUse hooks on the same tool each get a chance to evaluate the call; if any of them rejects it, the call is blocked. Here both independently would reject it — the point is the call doesn't execute, not which single hook 'wins.'

distractors.B: Registered hooks for an event aren't limited to just the first one — the whole point of registering multiple hooks is that each gets evaluated for a matching call.
distractors.C: Requiring every hook to reject before blocking would mean a call only needs one hook to approve it to bypass all enforcement — the opposite of how a safety mechanism should behave.
distractors.D: Multiple hooks on the same tool is a normal, supported configuration, not a conflict that causes enforcement to silently disappear.

scenario: A PreToolUse hook intended to redact PII from `lookup_order` results was registered globally (for all tools) instead of scoped to just `lookup_order`. It now also fires on unrelated tools like `get_shipping_rates`, adding latency and occasionally stripping legitimate numeric fields it mistakes for PII.
stem: What is the correct fix?

options.text: Scope the hook's registration to the specific tool(s) it's meant to apply to (`lookup_order`), rather than registering it globally for every tool call.
Leave the hook global, but add a check inside it for the string "order" somewhere in the response.
Remove the hook entirely, since PII redaction isn't worth the added latency.
Move the redaction logic into the system prompt instead of a hook.

rationale.correct: The defect is scope, not logic: a hook meant for one specific tool was registered to fire on every tool call. Scoping its registration to `lookup_order` specifically fixes both the wasted latency on unrelated tools and the false-positive redactions on data the hook was never meant to inspect.

distractors.B: Papering over an unscoped hook with a fragile string check inside it is a workaround, not a fix, and still runs the hook unnecessarily on every unrelated tool call.
distractors.C: PII redaction is exactly the kind of deterministic, safety-relevant requirement hooks exist for; removing it trades a scoping bug for no protection at all.
distractors.D: Moving deterministic redaction into a probabilistic prompt instruction reintroduces the exact reliability problem hooks are meant to solve.

scenario: A single customer message to the support agent contains three distinct issues: a refund request, a wrong shipping address, and a coupon that failed to apply.
stem: What is the best way to handle it?

options.text: Resolve the first issue and ask the customer to open separate tickets for the others.
Decompose the message into three items, investigate each (in parallel where possible) using shared context, then synthesize one unified resolution.
Escalate the whole conversation because multi-issue requests exceed the agent's scope.
Address only the issue whose wording sounds most urgent.

rationale.correct: Multi-concern requests should be decomposed into distinct items, each investigated against the shared conversational context, then synthesized into a single coherent resolution that addresses all three.

distractors.A: Shifting two of the three issues back onto the customer to file separately creates unnecessary friction and is not how decomposition should work.
distractors.C: Escalating the entire conversation is disproportionate; multi-issue requests are within scope once decomposed.
distractors.D: Picking only the most urgent-sounding issue silently drops legitimate parts of the request.

scenario: Researching ‘the state of renewable energy,’ every subagent in a research pipeline succeeds, yet the final reports cover only solar. The coordinator's logs show it decomposed the topic into ‘solar panel efficiency,’ ‘solar farm economics,’ and ‘residential solar,’ omitting wind, hydro, and geothermal.
stem: What is the root cause?

options.text: The search subagent's queries are not comprehensive enough.
The coordinator's task decomposition is too narrow, so subagent assignments miss whole domains of the topic.
The synthesis subagent is dropping non-solar findings.
The document-analysis subagent's relevance criteria are too restrictive.

rationale.correct: The logs implicate the coordinator directly: it never assigned wind, hydro, or geothermal subtopics in the first place, so downstream subagents executed correctly on an incomplete plan.

distractors.A: The search subagent only ran the queries it was assigned; it wasn't asked about wind, hydro, or geothermal at all.
distractors.C: There's nothing to drop — synthesis never received non-solar findings because they were never researched.
distractors.D: Document-analysis correctly analyzed the documents it was given; it was never asked to look at other energy types.

scenario: Midway through a fixed, pre-planned 5-step migration (steps decided upfront based on an initial audit), you discover the codebase has 3 additional call sites the original audit missed, in a module nobody expected to be affected.
stem: What should happen to the plan?

options.text: Revise the plan to add the newly discovered call sites as additional steps, since a decomposition plan is a living document that should be updated when new information invalidates its original assumptions.
Continue executing the original 5 steps exactly as planned and ignore the newly discovered call sites, since the plan was already fixed.
Restart the entire migration from scratch with a completely new plan.
Silently skip the newly discovered call sites since they weren't part of the original scope.

rationale.correct: A decomposition plan — even one initially treated as fixed — should be revised when new discoveries invalidate its original assumptions. The right move is updating the plan to cover the newly found call sites, not rigidly executing a plan now known to be incomplete.

distractors.B: Sticking to a plan now known to be incomplete leaves real work undone and produces an incomplete migration.
distractors.C: A full restart discards the valid progress already made on the original 5 steps; only the plan needs updating, not the whole effort.
distractors.D: Silently skipping newly discovered, in-scope work leaves the migration incomplete without anyone knowing.

scenario: A reviewer decomposes a 200-file review into 200 separate single-file passes, reasoning that maximum granularity guarantees maximum consistency. Coordination overhead balloons, and the reviewer still misses several bugs that only become visible when comparing groups of 4-5 related files that interact tightly (e.g., a model class and its four call sites).
stem: What is the actual problem with this decomposition?

options.text: The granularity is too fine for this codebase's structure — some genuinely related files need to be reviewed together (or cross-referenced by a targeted pass) to see interactions between them; splitting every single file into total isolation loses exactly those relationships.
Nothing is wrong; more granular decomposition always produces better results regardless of how files relate to each other.
The problem is only that 200 passes is too many API calls, unrelated to how the files were grouped.
The fix is to merge all 200 files back into a single pass to eliminate the coordination overhead.

rationale.correct: Decomposition granularity should reflect real structure in the work, not default to maximum fragmentation. When files interact tightly, splitting them into total isolation hides exactly the relationships that matter — the fix is grouping genuinely related files together (or adding a targeted cross-file pass for those groups), not just going finer or coarser uniformly.

distractors.B: Finer granularity isn't universally better — past the point where it matches real structure, it adds coordination cost while losing visibility into cross-file relationships, exactly as happened here.
distractors.C: The core issue is which files got grouped with which, not merely the raw count of API calls.
distractors.D: Collapsing back to one single pass reintroduces the original attention-dilution problem finer decomposition was meant to solve — the fix is better-chosen groupings, not abandoning decomposition.

scenario: A developer investigated a large codebase in a named session, then made substantial code changes, so the file contents captured in that session's tool results are now stale.
stem: What is the most reliable way to continue the work?

options.text: Resume the prior session with --resume and keep going.
Fork the session to create a branch from the prior analysis.
Start a new session and inject a structured summary of prior findings, noting which files changed.
Increase the context window so the stale results don't get dropped.

rationale.correct: When prior tool results are stale, starting fresh and injecting a structured summary of what was found (and what changed) is more reliable than resuming, which would carry the stale results forward as if they were still current.

distractors.A: Resuming with --resume keeps the stale tool results in context, exactly the problem to avoid.
distractors.B: Forking also inherits the stale baseline from the prior session.
distractors.D: A larger context window preserves the stale data rather than correcting it.

scenario: A session's accumulated context is still entirely valid and directly relevant — nothing is stale — but after three days of deep exploration it has grown so large that you're near the context window limit, and the next request risks truncating older, still-important findings.
stem: What is the best way to proceed?

options.text: Start a fresh session and inject a distilled summary of the key findings, even though nothing is stale, since the actual constraint here is context budget, not validity — carrying the full accumulated history forward risks losing information to truncation.
Keep resuming the same session indefinitely, since all the context is still valid and staleness is the only reason to ever start fresh.
Run `/compact` repeatedly until the session fits, and treat that as a permanent solution rather than eventually needing a fresh start.
Delete the oldest half of the conversation history to make room, without summarizing it first.

rationale.correct: Validity and context budget are two separate constraints. Even fully valid context can outgrow the window; when that happens, the practical fix is the same as for staleness — start fresh with a distilled summary — just for a different reason (size, not staleness).

distractors.B: Treating staleness as the only valid reason to start fresh ignores the very real constraint of running out of context room, which is happening here regardless of validity.
distractors.C: Repeated compaction is lossy and, used as a permanent strategy rather than an occasional tool, degrades the very findings you're trying to preserve.
distractors.D: Deleting history without summarizing it first discards findings outright instead of preserving them in condensed form.

scenario: A team of five engineers all resume Claude Code sessions by whatever name they happened to type when starting them ('test', 'fix', 'session2'), making it impossible for anyone to find or resume a teammate's prior investigation of a specific bug or feature.
stem: What convention would most directly fix this?

options.text: Adopt a consistent, descriptive session-naming convention (e.g., including the ticket ID or feature name) when starting a named session, so any teammate can identify and resume the right one later.
Have everyone use the exact same session name so all investigations share one session.
Disable named sessions entirely and always start fresh for every task.
Have engineers email each other their session names whenever needed, without changing the naming pattern itself.

rationale.correct: The problem is that names carry no identifying information. A descriptive naming convention (ticket ID, feature, or bug reference) is what makes a named session discoverable and resumable by someone other than the person who started it.

distractors.B: Sharing one name across all investigations would mix unrelated work into a single session, the opposite of what's needed.
distractors.C: Disabling named sessions throws away the resumption mechanism entirely rather than fixing how sessions are named.
distractors.D: Ad hoc communication about session names doesn't scale and doesn't fix the underlying discoverability problem — it just works around it case by case.

scenario: You have a session with a solid, validated understanding of a payment service's architecture. You're about to try a risky, exploratory refactor and want to preserve the validated baseline exactly as-is in case the exploration goes badly, while still building on top of everything already learned.
stem: What is the best way to proceed?

options.text: Fork the session before starting the risky exploration, so the original stays untouched as a clean checkpoint while the fork inherits the full validated baseline and absorbs any exploratory dead ends.
Continue directly in the original session, since nothing bad has happened yet.
Start an entirely fresh session with no prior context, to avoid any risk to the original.
Manually copy notes about the architecture into a text file before proceeding, then continue in the original session anyway.

rationale.correct: Forking is exactly for this: preserving a validated baseline session untouched while a new branch — which inherits everything already learned — takes on the risk of an exploratory path that might not pan out.

distractors.B: Continuing directly in the original session means a bad exploratory turn contaminates the very session you wanted to preserve as a clean checkpoint.
distractors.C: Starting with no prior context throws away the validated architectural understanding you explicitly want to keep building on.
distractors.D: Manual note-copying doesn't actually protect the live session from the risky changes you're about to make in it, and loses the richer context a real fork preserves.

scenario: After enriching two similar tools' descriptions with formats, examples, and disambiguating guidance, the agent still occasionally calls the wrong one for genuinely ambiguous requests.
stem: What is the appropriate next step, given the first-step remedy (better descriptions) hasn't fully resolved it?

options.text: Immediately merge the two tools into one, since any remaining confusion means they should never have been separate.
Add a few-shot example set specifically covering the genuinely ambiguous request patterns that still cause misrouting, layered on top of the improved descriptions.
Revert the description changes, since they clearly didn't work.
Add a hidden keyword-matching router in front of the model to force tool selection outside the model's own reasoning.

rationale.correct: When enriched descriptions close most but not all of the gap, targeted few-shot examples for the specific remaining ambiguous patterns are the next proportionate step — it builds on the improved descriptions rather than discarding them or reaching for a heavier-handed fix.

distractors.A: Merging is a larger architectural change that should follow, not precede, exhausting cheaper fixes like targeted examples.
distractors.C: Reverting a fix that measurably reduced (even if it didn't eliminate) misrouting discards real progress.
distractors.D: A hidden router bypasses the model's own tool-selection reasoning entirely, which is a heavier, less flexible intervention than examples for the remaining edge cases.

scenario: A coding agent keeps using the built-in Grep tool instead of a team's more capable MCP code-search tool.
stem: What is the best fix?

options.text: Remove the agent's access to Grep entirely.
Enhance the MCP tool's description to clearly explain its capabilities and outputs so the agent prefers it.
Rename the built-in Grep tool.
Force tool_choice to the MCP tool on every turn.

rationale.correct: Enhancing the MCP tool's description so its capabilities and outputs are clear leads the model to prefer it over the built-in when it's genuinely the better choice, addressing the root cause of the selection problem.

distractors.A: Removing Grep entirely is heavy-handed and removes a tool that's still useful for some turns.
distractors.C: Renaming Grep doesn't communicate anything about the MCP tool's actual value.
distractors.D: Forcing tool_choice to the MCP tool on every turn is inflexible for turns where Grep is genuinely the better fit.

scenario: A `send_email` tool's description has grown to 400 words covering every edge case, historical context, and internal implementation detail the team has ever debated, in addition to its actual purpose and usage.
stem: What is the most likely effect on tool selection, and what should you do?

options.text: The verbosity itself can dilute the model's attention on the actually decision-relevant details (purpose, inputs, when to use it); trim the description to the essential purpose, inputs, and disambiguating guidance, moving historical/implementation notes elsewhere.
Longer descriptions always improve selection reliability, since more information can only help the model decide correctly.
Description length has no effect on tool selection; only the tool's name matters.
The description should be split across multiple tools, one per edge case mentioned.

rationale.correct: Tool descriptions are attention-limited context, not an unlimited reference document — burying the decision-relevant purpose and usage guidance under historical and implementation detail makes it harder, not easier, for the model to extract what actually matters for selection. A tight, purpose-focused description usually selects better than an exhaustive one.

distractors.B: More text is not strictly better; past a point, added length adds noise that competes with the decision-relevant content for the model's attention.
distractors.C: Descriptions are the primary selection signal alongside the name; claiming length is irrelevant contradicts that.
distractors.D: Splitting into multiple tools per edge case fragments a single real capability into artificial ones, which is a different (and unwarranted) problem than trimming a bloated description.

scenario: Your platform has five `get_*` tools (`get_user`, `get_order`, `get_invoice`, `get_shipment`, `get_refund`). Four follow the pattern "Retrieves a <noun> by ID and returns <fields>"; the fifth, `get_refund`, instead says "Refund lookup utility."
stem: What is the most likely consequence of this inconsistency, and the best fix?

options.text: The odd-one-out description gives the model less to work with than its siblings, making `get_refund` comparatively harder to select correctly; rewrite it to match the family's pattern (retrieves-by-ID plus returned fields).
No consequence — as long as each individual description is accurate, consistency across the family doesn't matter.
Rename `get_refund` to `get_refund_v2` to signal it works differently.
Remove the other four tools' consistent phrasing so all five match the informal style of `get_refund`.

rationale.correct: Even an individually-reasonable description can under-inform selection relative to its siblings — the sparse, informal phrasing on `get_refund` gives the model less to differentiate it by within an otherwise well-specified family. Matching the established pattern (identifying key, and returned fields) restores that signal.

distractors.B: Consistency matters because the model is choosing among all five together; a comparatively thin description makes that one relatively easy to overlook or misuse even if it's not wrong in isolation.
distractors.C: A version-style rename doesn't add the missing information about what the tool retrieves or returns.
distractors.D: Downgrading the four well-specified descriptions to match the weakest one makes selection worse for the whole family, not better.

scenario: A `bulk_update_inventory` MCP tool processes a batch of 50 SKU updates in one call. 47 succeed; 3 fail because those SKUs don't exist in the catalog.
stem: How should the tool report this back to the calling agent?

options.text: Return a structured response listing per-item results — which SKUs succeeded, and for each failed SKU, the specific reason — rather than a single pass/fail verdict for the whole batch.
Return `isError: true` for the whole call, since 3 of 50 items failed.
Return `isError: false` and silently drop the 3 failed items from the response.
Retry the entire batch of 50 automatically until all 50 succeed.

rationale.correct: A partial-batch outcome isn't a single success or failure — the agent needs per-item visibility to know exactly which 3 SKUs need attention and why, while correctly treating the other 47 as done. A single aggregate verdict in either direction loses that information.

distractors.B: Marking the whole call as an error obscures that 47 items genuinely succeeded and don't need to be redone.
distractors.C: Silently dropping the failed items hides real problems (SKUs needing catalog correction) from the agent and the user.
distractors.D: Blindly retrying the whole batch re-does 47 already-successful updates and will fail identically on the 3 nonexistent SKUs every time, since retrying doesn't fix a data problem.

scenario: A `send_notification` MCP tool starts returning failures once a client exceeds 100 calls per minute against the notification provider's API.
stem: How should this failure be categorized and communicated so the agent handles it well?

options.text: As a distinct, retryable rate-limit category (not a generic transient error) including a `retryAfter` value, so the agent waits the right amount of time instead of retrying immediately or treating it as a hard failure.
As a business-rule failure with `retriable: false`, since the limit is a fixed policy.
As a generic `isError: true` with no further detail, same as any other failure.
As a successful call with an empty result, since the notification will eventually succeed once the rate limit resets.

rationale.correct: Rate limiting is retryable, but immediate retries make it worse, and generic-transient handling (retry right away) doesn't respect the provider's actual reset window. A dedicated category plus a concrete wait-time signal (`retryAfter`) lets the agent retry correctly instead of guessing.

distractors.B: Marking it non-retryable is wrong — the call will succeed later, once the window resets; that's exactly what distinguishes rate limiting from a hard business rule.
distractors.C: A generic, undifferentiated error throws away the one piece of information (how long to wait) that would let the agent recover cleanly.
distractors.D: Reporting a rate-limited call as successful is inaccurate — the notification was not sent, and the agent needs to know that to decide whether/when to retry.

scenario: A `delete_repository` MCP tool fails because the calling user's token lacks the required admin scope. This is different from the tool being temporarily unreachable, and different from a business-rule rejection like 'repository has open PRs.'
stem: How should this failure be categorized, and what should the agent do with it?

options.text: As a distinct permission/authorization category, non-retryable by the agent itself — surface it to the user or a human with enough detail to know which permission is missing, rather than retrying or silently failing.
As a transient failure, since retrying with backoff will eventually succeed.
As a business-rule failure identical to 'repository has open PRs,' since both block the same action.
As a successful no-op, since nothing was deleted.

rationale.correct: A missing permission won't resolve itself through retries the way a transient failure would, and it's a different kind of blocker than a business rule the requester could satisfy themselves (like closing PRs first) — it needs a human with the right access to act. Categorizing it distinctly, and being specific about what's missing, is what lets the right actor (not the agent) resolve it.

distractors.B: No amount of retrying grants a token more scope; treating this as transient wastes calls and time.
distractors.C: Conflating a permissions gap with a satisfiable business rule misleads the agent about what would actually unblock the action — a user can close PRs themselves, but can't grant themselves admin scope.
distractors.D: Silently treating a blocked, unauthorized deletion as a successful no-op hides a real problem that needs a person's attention.

scenario: A `charge_card` MCP tool sends a charge request, but the network connection drops before the response arrives. The tool cannot tell whether the charge actually completed on the payment provider's side before the connection failed.
stem: How should the tool respond, and what should the agent do?

options.text: Return a distinct 'outcome unknown' status (not a plain success or failure) and have the agent check the actual charge status via an idempotency key or a status-check call before deciding whether to retry — never blindly resubmit a payment whose outcome is unconfirmed.
Return `isError: true` and let the agent retry the charge immediately, since a failed network call means the charge didn't happen.
Return `isError: false`, since the request was sent even though the response never arrived.
Ignore the ambiguity and have the agent proceed with the rest of its workflow as if the charge succeeded.

rationale.correct: For an action with real-world side effects like a charge, a dropped connection after the request was sent is genuinely ambiguous — the charge may have gone through. Blindly retrying risks a double charge, and blindly assuming success or failure risks either a lost charge or a duplicate one. The safe pattern is an explicit 'unknown' outcome plus an idempotent way to check or safely resubmit.

distractors.B: Assuming failure and retrying immediately risks charging the customer twice if the original request actually succeeded before the connection dropped.
distractors.C: Assuming success when the actual outcome is unconfirmed risks the agent proceeding as if payment was received when it may not have been.
distractors.D: Proceeding as if the charge succeeded, without resolving the ambiguity, risks the workflow completing on a false assumption for a financially consequential action.

scenario: An agent legitimately needs access to most of an 18-tool platform across different request types, but selection reliability suffers whenever all 18 are available at once.
stem: What design best preserves broad capability while restoring selection reliability?

options.text: Keep all 18 tools available on every turn and accept the selection-reliability cost as unavoidable.
Classify each incoming request by type first, then expose only the subset of tools relevant to that request type for the turn.
Remove least-used tools permanently, regardless of whether some request types still need them.
Add few-shot examples covering all 18 tools to compensate.

rationale.correct: Dynamically scoping which tools are exposed per request type keeps the full capability available across the system while never presenting the model with more choices than a given turn actually needs — directly addressing the decision-complexity problem instead of trading away capability or patching around it.

distractors.A: Accepting the cost when a structural fix is available ignores a well-understood, addressable problem.
distractors.C: Permanently removing tools some request types still need trades away real capability instead of fixing the selection problem.
distractors.D: Examples for all 18 tools add prompt overhead without reducing the decision complexity of choosing among that many options on a single turn.

scenario: For a specific diagnostic turn, you want the model to respond with a plain-text explanation only, guaranteed not to call any tool, even though several tools are configured and available.
stem: Which `tool_choice` setting achieves this?

options.text: `tool_choice: "none"`, which prevents any tool call and forces a text-only response for that turn.
`tool_choice: "auto"`, since the model will usually choose not to call a tool if none is needed.
Remove all tools from the request temporarily.
`tool_choice: "any"`, which allows the broadest set of tool options.

rationale.correct: `tool_choice: "none"` is the explicit setting for guaranteeing a text-only response — it disables tool calling for that turn without requiring you to remove and re-add the tool definitions.

distractors.B: "auto" leaves the choice to the model each turn; it doesn't guarantee a tool won't be called, which is exactly the guarantee needed here.
distractors.C: Removing tool definitions works but is a heavier-handed, stateful workaround compared to the purpose-built setting.
distractors.D: "any" does the opposite of what's wanted — it guarantees a tool IS called.

scenario: A team forces `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}` on every single turn of a multi-turn coding-assistant conversation, reasoning that 'forcing a tool guarantees structured, reliable behavior.' Users now report the assistant tries to extract metadata even when they ask an unrelated question like 'explain this error message.'
stem: What is the mistake in this design, and what should change?

options.text: Forcing one specific tool call on every turn removes the model's ability to respond conversationally or pick a different, more appropriate tool when the request doesn't call for that specific action; reserve forced tool_choice for the narrow turns that genuinely require it, and use `auto` (or an unforced `any`) elsewhere.
Nothing is wrong; forcing a specific tool is always the safest, most reliable choice for every turn in any application.
The fix is to rename `extract_metadata` to something more general so it can answer any question.
The fix is to force a different single tool instead, so at least one tool always runs.

rationale.correct: Forced tool_choice is a narrow-purpose setting for turns where you genuinely need that exact action to happen — applying it blanket-wide removes the model's ability to have an ordinary conversation or select the tool actually suited to a given request, exactly the failure mode reported.

distractors.B: Blanket forcing is precisely what's causing the reported failures; it is not a universally safe default.
distractors.C: Renaming the tool doesn't change what it does; it still can't meaningfully answer unrelated questions like explaining an error message.
distractors.D: Swapping which single tool is forced doesn't fix the underlying problem of forcing one tool on every turn regardless of what's actually being asked.

scenario: An agent with `search_flights` and `search_hotels` tools is asked to look up both flight and hotel options for a trip in one request. You want both searches to run together rather than one after the other, and today's behavior is inconsistent — sometimes parallel, sometimes sequential.
stem: What is the most direct way to make simultaneous tool calls the reliable default here?

options.text: Configure the request so parallel tool use isn't disabled (leave the model free to emit multiple tool_use blocks in one turn) and prompt the assistant to call both searches together when a request calls for independent lookups.
Set `tool_choice` to force `search_flights` specifically, since forcing one tool guarantees both will run.
Rename the tools so they sort alphabetically next to each other.
Increase `max_tokens` so there's room for two tool calls.

rationale.correct: Simultaneous tool calls happen when the model emits multiple `tool_use` blocks in one turn, which requires that parallel tool use is available (not disabled) and that the prompt/task makes clear both independent lookups are wanted together — that's the direct lever for consistent parallel behavior.

distractors.B: Forcing one specific tool only guarantees that one tool is called; it says nothing about a second, different tool running alongside it.
distractors.C: Naming/sort order has no bearing on whether the model emits one or multiple tool_use blocks in a turn.
distractors.D: max_tokens controls output length, not whether the model chooses to call one or multiple tools in the same turn.

scenario: You're designing an MCP server for a wiki. Some data is quasi-static reference material (the page index, category taxonomy) that rarely changes; other functionality requires the agent to actively search page content by keyword, or create and update pages.
stem: How should you split this between MCP resources and MCP tools?

options.text: Expose the static page index and category taxonomy as resources (so the agent can see them without a tool call), and expose search, create, and update actions as tools (since those require dynamic input the agent supplies each time).
Expose everything as tools, since tools are the only mechanism MCP provides for making data available to an agent.
Expose everything as resources, including search and update actions, so the agent has full visibility with no tool-calling overhead.
Expose the page index as a tool the agent calls once per session, and put search/update behind resources instead.

rationale.correct: Resources are the right fit for stable, browsable reference content the agent should have visibility into without spending a tool call — exactly the page index and taxonomy here. Actions that need per-call, dynamic input (a search query, new page content) are what tools are for.

distractors.B: Tools aren't the only mechanism — that's exactly the design flaw resources exist to fix, and using tools for stable reference data adds needless exploratory calls.
distractors.C: Search and update are actions with per-call inputs and side effects (for update); resources are read-only content, not a substitute for actions.
distractors.D: This inverts the correct assignment — the stable index is what benefits from resource-style visibility, and the dynamic actions are what need tool semantics.

scenario: A well-known community MCP server for your CRM hasn't been updated in two years, has several open security issues, and doesn't support your CRM's newer API version, which your team needs.
stem: Given the general guidance to prefer community servers for standard integrations, what should you do here?

options.text: Build (or fork and update) a custom server anyway, since an unmaintained, insecure, or feature-incomplete community server no longer represents the low-risk, well-solved option the general guidance assumes.
Use the community server as-is, since community servers should always be preferred over custom ones regardless of their maintenance state.
Skip MCP entirely and call the CRM's REST API directly from the agent.
Expose the CRM only as an MCP resource, with no tools, to avoid the security issues.

rationale.correct: The 'prefer community servers' guidance is a default for well-maintained, standard integrations — it assumes reasonable security and feature parity. When a community server is stale, insecure, or missing needed capabilities, those assumptions no longer hold, and building or updating a custom server is the right call.

distractors.B: Treating 'prefer community' as an absolute rule ignores the very problems described — an outdated, insecure, or incomplete server is not actually the safe default anymore.
distractors.C: Bypassing MCP entirely loses the standardized tool-discovery and integration benefits MCP provides, and doesn't address the underlying need for a properly integrated server.
distractors.D: A resource-only exposure can't perform the write/update actions CRM work typically requires, and doesn't solve the security or version gaps either.

scenario: A project's `.mcp.json` configures a GitHub MCP server and a Postgres MCP server. Today, the Postgres server's host is down for maintenance. A developer starts a session needing only the GitHub tools.
stem: What should happen, ideally?

options.text: The session should still start with the GitHub tools available and working; the Postgres server's unavailability should be reported (e.g., a connection warning) without blocking access to the other, healthy server's tools.
The whole session should refuse to start until every configured MCP server, including Postgres, is reachable.
The GitHub server should also be marked unavailable, since one server in the config is down.
Remove Postgres from `.mcp.json` permanently so the team never has to consider it again.

rationale.correct: MCP servers are configured and connected independently; one server being temporarily unreachable shouldn't cascade into blocking access to a different, healthy server's tools the developer doesn't even need right now.

distractors.B: Requiring every configured server to be reachable before starting turns one server's routine maintenance window into an outage for unrelated work.
distractors.C: There's no dependency between separately-configured servers; one being down doesn't imply anything is wrong with another.
distractors.D: Permanently removing a server over a temporary maintenance window discards real, working configuration the team still needs.

scenario: Your project configures two MCP servers, each of which happens to expose a tool literally named `search`: one searches internal documentation, the other searches a customer database. Both are connected in the same session.
stem: What is the most direct way to avoid the agent confusing the two `search` tools?

options.text: Configure or request that each server expose its tool under a distinct, descriptive name (or rely on the client's namespacing of tools by server, where supported), so the agent sees two clearly distinguishable tools rather than two identically-named ones.
Disconnect one of the two servers whenever the other is needed, so only one `search` tool is ever available at a time.
Instruct the agent, in the system prompt, to always guess based on context which `search` it means.
Rename the servers (not the tools) in `.mcp.json`, since server names are what the model uses to disambiguate tool calls.

rationale.correct: Two identically-named tools give the model nothing to differentiate them by at the point of selection; distinct, descriptive tool names (or client-level namespacing where available) restore a clear selection signal, the same underlying principle as any other under-differentiated tool pair.

distractors.B: Manually toggling server connections to avoid a naming collision is a heavy, error-prone workaround for what a better name fixes directly.
distractors.C: Asking the model to guess from context reintroduces exactly the ambiguity a clear name would eliminate outright.
distractors.D: The model selects among tool definitions (names/descriptions), not server config names; renaming only the server doesn't change what the model actually sees.

scenario: You want to find every `TODO` comment left in the codebase before a release, regardless of which file or language they're in.
stem: Which built-in tool is the right choice?

options.text: Grep for the string `TODO`.
Glob with a pattern like `**/*.md`.
Read every file and scan visually for `TODO`.
Bash with a recursive `ls`.

rationale.correct: Grep searches file contents for a text pattern regardless of file type or location, which is exactly what's needed to find every occurrence of a comment marker like `TODO` across the whole codebase.

distractors.B: Glob only matches file paths/names by pattern; `**/*.md` would also incorrectly restrict the search to markdown files, missing TODOs in code.
distractors.C: Reading every file to scan manually is far less efficient than a single targeted content search.
distractors.D: A recursive directory listing enumerates file paths; it doesn't search inside file contents at all.

scenario: You need to find every `Dockerfile` in a monorepo containing dozens of services, regardless of how deeply nested each service's directory is.
stem: Which built-in tool fits best?

options.text: Grep for the string "FROM" (a line every Dockerfile contains).
Glob with `**/Dockerfile`.
Read the top-level directory listing.
Bash with `find` piped through several `grep` stages.

rationale.correct: Glob matches files by name/path pattern regardless of nesting depth; `**/Dockerfile` finds every file with that exact name at any depth, which is exactly the naming-convention search this calls for.

distractors.A: Searching for a common line like `FROM` searches contents, and risks false positives/negatives depending on file conventions — it's solving the wrong problem when the actual ask is finding files by name.
distractors.C: The top-level listing won't surface Dockerfiles nested inside each service's own subdirectory.
distractors.D: Chaining `find` and `grep` through Bash reinvents what Glob already does directly and more reliably.

scenario: You need to run the project's existing test suite (`npm test`) and view the output to confirm a fix works.
stem: Which built-in tool is appropriate here?

options.text: Bash, to execute the existing test command directly.
Edit, to modify the test files so they print their own results.
Grep, to search test files for assertions.
Write, to create a new test-runner script from scratch.

rationale.correct: Running an existing shell command like a test suite is exactly what Bash is for — it executes commands and returns their output, with no need to touch any files at all.

distractors.B: Editing test files to change how they print doesn't run them, and needlessly modifies source you don't need to touch.
distractors.C: Grep searches file contents; it can't execute anything or report live test results.
distractors.D: Writing a brand-new runner from scratch reinvents infrastructure that already exists and works.

scenario: You need to create a brand-new configuration file, `config/feature-flags.json`, that doesn't exist yet in the repository.
stem: Which built-in tool is the right choice?

options.text: Write, to create the new file with its initial contents.
Edit, anchored on the file's expected first line.
Grep, to confirm the file doesn't already exist.
Glob, to generate the file from a pattern.

rationale.correct: Write creates a file (or fully overwrites one); since this file doesn't exist yet, there's no existing content to anchor an Edit against — Write is the direct, correct tool for creating new file content.

distractors.B: Edit modifies existing text by matching an anchor already present in the file; there's nothing to anchor on in a file that doesn't exist yet.
distractors.C: Grep searches existing file contents; it can't confirm non-existence of a path or create anything.
distractors.D: Glob matches existing file paths by pattern; it doesn't generate or create file content.

scenario: A team's root CLAUDE.md documents a shared testing convention. One engineer also has a personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md with unrelated formatting preferences. A new teammate reports that Claude follows the testing convention but seems unaware of an unwritten 'always confirm before deleting files' habit the original engineer has relied on.
stem: What is the most likely explanation for the missing 'confirm before deleting' behavior?

options.text: That habit was never actually written into either CLAUDE.md file — it existed only as the original engineer's manual practice, not as configuration at all.
It must be in the personal ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and failed to propagate, the same failure mode as any user-level instruction.
Claude Code only loads one CLAUDE.md file per session, so the personal file's instructions were silently dropped in favor of the project file.
The new teammate needs to run /compact to load the missing instruction.

rationale.correct: If the behavior only ever existed as the original engineer's manual habit and was never actually written into any CLAUDE.md, there is no configuration file — user- or project-level — for a new teammate to be missing. The fix is to write it down (in the project file, if it should be shared), not to look for a propagation bug.

distractors.B: This assumes the habit was written into the personal file at all, which isn't established — it may never have been captured as an instruction anywhere.
distractors.C: Claude Code loads multiple applicable memory files together (e.g., project and user-level); it does not restrict itself to just one.
distractors.D: /compact summarizes conversation history and has no role in loading configuration files.

scenario: CI-generated tests are low-value and ignore a project's established fixtures and testing standards.
stem: What most improves generation quality?

options.text: Increase max_tokens so more tests are generated.
Document testing standards, valuable-test criteria, and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md so CI-invoked Claude uses them.
Switch test generation to the Message Batches API.
Ask for more tests per run.

rationale.correct: CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for supplying project context — standards, fixtures, and criteria — to CI-invoked Claude, which raises test quality rather than just volume.

distractors.A: More tokens increases how much can be generated, not whether it's actually valuable.
distractors.C: Batch processing affects cost and latency, not test relevance or quality.
distractors.D: Asking for more tests per run increases volume in the same way option A does, without addressing quality.

scenario: A project's root CLAUDE.md still instructs Claude Code to 'use the legacy /api/v1 endpoints for all HTTP calls,' but the team fully migrated to /api/v2 six months ago and removed v1 entirely.
stem: What is the most direct problem this causes, and the correct fix?

options.text: Claude Code will keep following the stale instruction as written (it has no way to know it's outdated), generating code against a removed API; update CLAUDE.md to reflect the current v2 endpoints as part of ordinary maintenance whenever conventions change.
Claude Code automatically detects when project conventions have changed and ignores outdated instructions.
CLAUDE.md instructions expire automatically after a fixed period and stop applying.
Nothing — Claude Code always double-checks instructions against the actual codebase before following them.

rationale.correct: CLAUDE.md is followed as written; it has no independent way to detect that the codebase has moved on. Like any other documentation, it needs to be kept in sync with reality — the responsibility for updating it after a migration falls on the team, not the tool.

distractors.B: There's no such automatic-detection mechanism; CLAUDE.md content is taken as given.
distractors.C: Instructions in CLAUDE.md don't have a built-in expiration; stale content persists until someone updates it.
distractors.D: Claude Code doesn't independently verify CLAUDE.md's claims against the codebase before following them; that's exactly why stale instructions cause real problems.

scenario: A monorepo has a root CLAUDE.md, a `services/CLAUDE.md`, and a `services/payments/CLAUDE.md`. All three say something about logging: root says 'use structured JSON logs,' `services/CLAUDE.md` says 'include a request_id field,' and `services/payments/CLAUDE.md` says 'also include a masked account_id field.'
stem: When editing a file inside `services/payments/`, which logging guidance applies?

options.text: All three, combined additively: structured JSON logs, with a request_id field, and also a masked account_id field — each level adds to the ones above it rather than replacing them.
Only `services/payments/CLAUDE.md`'s guidance, since the most specific file overrides the broader ones entirely.
Only the root CLAUDE.md's guidance, since it is loaded first.
Whichever file was edited most recently.

rationale.correct: CLAUDE.md files are hierarchical and additive — instructions from the root, intermediate, and most specific directory-level files all combine into the effective context for a given path, rather than the most specific one replacing the others.

distractors.B: Directory-level files add to broader ones; they don't erase guidance from parent levels.
distractors.C: The root file's guidance still applies; it's just supplemented, not the only thing in effect.
distractors.D: Effective instructions are determined by directory hierarchy relative to the file being edited, not by which file was edited most recently.

scenario: A team's shared /deploy command in .claude/commands/ works for everyone, but one engineer wants to add a few personal extra safety checks on top of it for their own local runs, without changing the shared version teammates rely on.
stem: What is the recommended way to layer a personal variant on top of a shared command?

options.text: Edit the shared .claude/commands/deploy.md directly to add the extra checks, since that file already ships with the repo.
Create a personal command with a different name in ~/.claude/commands/ that wraps or extends the shared behavior for this engineer's own use.
Ask every teammate to individually decide whether they want the extra checks, edited into the same shared file.
There is no supported way to have both; the engineer must choose either the shared command or a fully separate personal one with no relationship to it.

rationale.correct: A personal, differently-named command in the user-level ~/.claude/commands/ directory lets one engineer layer their own extra checks without touching the shared, version-controlled command everyone else depends on.

distractors.A: Editing the shared file directly imposes one engineer's personal preference on the whole team.
distractors.C: Baking an individual's preference into the shared file conflates personal and team configuration instead of separating them.
distractors.D: A personal command can still be designed to build on or reference the shared one's intent; this isn't an all-or-nothing choice.

scenario: You want a `security-scan` skill to run automatically whenever Claude judges that a change touches security-sensitive code, without anyone needing to remember to invoke it by name.
stem: What determines whether Claude invokes this skill automatically?

options.text: The quality and specificity of the skill's `description` field, since Claude decides whether to invoke a skill by matching the current context against its description.
Setting `disable-model-invocation: true` in the skill's frontmatter.
Adding `context: fork` so the skill activates during any security-relevant reasoning step.
Adding an `argument-hint` describing when the skill applies.
