options.text: No — the customer's opinion about the policy's clarity is not one of the defined escalation triggers (explicit request, policy gap, capability limit, or genuine stall); the request itself is standard and within the agent's authority, so it should simply be processed.
Yes, because any negative comment about the company should be escalated to protect the customer relationship.
Yes, because mentioning confusion about a policy always signals a policy gap requiring escalation.
Yes, out of caution, since escalating unnecessary cases is always the safer default regardless of cost to resolution speed.

rationale.correct: A passing negative opinion about clarity, on an otherwise completely standard and in-scope request, isn't one of the actual escalation triggers — there's no explicit request for a human, no real policy gap (the return itself is squarely covered), no capability limit, and no stall. The proportionate response is to just process the standard return.

distractors.B: A single negative comment isn't itself an escalation trigger; treating any complaint as one would escalate far more cases than warranted.
distractors.C: The customer isn't describing an actual gap in what the policy covers — the return itself is standard and covered; a passing remark about clarity isn't the same as the policy failing to address the situation.
distractors.D: Escalating cases outside the actual defined triggers isn't 'safer' — it wastes scarce human capacity on cases the agent can and should resolve, without materially reducing risk.

scenario: A coordinator delegates to subagent B, which itself delegates a sub-task to subagent C. Subagent C fails with a structured error (failure type, attempted query, partial results). Subagent B currently catches C's failure and reports back to the coordinator only a bare 'sub-task failed' string, discarding C's structured detail.
stem: What is the problem, and the fix?

options.text: Structured error detail is being discarded at the intermediate hop; subagent B should forward (or meaningfully summarize while preserving) C's structured context to the coordinator, not collapse it into a generic string, the same principle that applies to a single hop.
This is fine, since the coordinator only needs to know that something, somewhere, failed.
Subagent B should silently retry C's failed sub-task itself, without ever informing the coordinator anything happened.
Subagent C should have propagated its error directly to the coordinator instead of going through B.

rationale.correct: The same principle that governs propagation to a coordinator applies at every hop: collapsing structured detail into a generic string strips the coordinator of the information it needs to decide how to recover, regardless of how many hops the error passed through to get there.

distractors.B: The coordinator's ability to make an intelligent recovery decision depends on the structured detail, not just the bare fact that a failure occurred somewhere.
distractors.C: Silently retrying without informing the coordinator hides a real event from the level that's supposed to have visibility into recoverable failures.
distractors.D: The delegation structure means C reports to B, which reports to the coordinator; the fix is for B to preserve C's detail when forwarding, not to bypass the actual chain of delegation.

scenario: A document-processing subagent's internal work has three steps: fetch the document, extract structured fields, and validate the extraction. On one run, fetch and extract succeed, but validation fails.
stem: How should the subagent report this to the coordinator?

options.text: Report which of its internal steps succeeded and which failed (fetch: ok, extract: ok, validate: failed, with the validation error detail), not just a single overall pass/fail — so the coordinator knows the extracted data exists and only validation needs attention.
Report only a single overall 'failed' status, since one internal step failed.
Report only a single overall 'succeeded' status, since two of the three steps worked.
Discard the successfully extracted data along with the failure, since the run as a whole didn't fully complete.

rationale.correct: Collapsing a three-step internal process into one bare pass/fail loses exactly the information (which step failed, and that the earlier successful work still exists) the coordinator needs — reporting per-step outcomes gives it a much more useful, actionable picture.

distractors.B: A single 'failed' status obscures that real, usable work (the extraction) actually completed before the failure.
distractors.C: Calling the whole run a 'success' when validation genuinely failed misrepresents what actually happened and could let bad data flow downstream unflagged.
distractors.D: Discarding a successful extraction that already happened wastes real, valid work over an unrelated step's failure.

scenario: A coordinator retries a subagent call after a transient timeout. The retry also times out, with an identical failure type and query. The subagent reports this second timeout as a completely fresh, unrelated failure event, with no reference to the fact that this is the second consecutive occurrence of the same failure on the same request.
stem: What is missing, and why does it matter?

options.text: A signal that this is a repeat of the same underlying failure (e.g., a retry count or reference to the prior attempt), which matters because the coordinator needs to distinguish 'first transient hiccup, worth one more retry' from 'this specific request keeps failing the same way, retrying again probably won't help' before deciding what to do next.
Nothing is missing; each failure should always be treated as entirely independent regardless of how many times the same thing has just happened.
The subagent should stop reporting failures altogether after the first one.
The coordinator should ignore all failure reports after the first, since repeated timeouts are expected and unimportant.

rationale.correct: Without a signal that this is the same failure recurring, the coordinator can't tell a one-off transient hiccup from a request that's genuinely stuck failing the same way — that distinction is exactly what should inform whether another retry is worth attempting or whether it's time to try something else.

distractors.B: Treating every retry failure as brand-new information discards the pattern (repeated identical failures on the same request) that's actually useful for deciding whether to keep retrying.
distractors.C: Suppressing failure reporting after the first occurrence hides real, ongoing problems from the coordinator.
distractors.D: Ignoring repeated failure reports treats a potentially escalating problem (a request that keeps failing) as unimportant, when it's exactly the kind of signal that should inform a different recovery decision.

scenario: A subagent's structured error report shows: failure_type is 'permission_denied' — the credentials the agent was given don't have access to a data source it needs. This isn't something a different query, a retry, or an alternative subagent approach can work around; the actual permission grant itself needs to change.
stem: What should the coordinator do with this error?

options.text: Recognize that this specific failure type can't be resolved by any action available to the agents themselves (retry, alternative query, partial results) and escalate it to a human who can actually grant or verify the needed access, rather than looping on approaches that can't succeed.
Keep retrying with different query phrasings, since eventually one might bypass the permission requirement.
Silently proceed without that data source and present the result as if nothing was missing.
Have a different subagent attempt the exact same request with the exact same credentials, hoping for a different outcome.

rationale.correct: A permissions gap isn't the kind of failure that any amount of retrying, rephrasing, or trying a different subagent can fix — the actual constraint (insufficient access) doesn't change based on the approach taken. Recognizing which failure types are genuinely un-fixable by agent-level actions, and escalating those specifically to a human who controls access, is the correct behavior.

distractors.B: No query phrasing works around an actual permissions restriction; retrying different wording doesn't change what credentials are actually authorized to access.
distractors.C: Silently omitting the data and presenting the result as complete hides a real gap from whoever relies on the output.
distractors.D: The same credentials will hit the same permission wall regardless of which subagent presents the request; changing which agent asks doesn't change what it's authorized to see.

scenario: A developer needs to build an accurate mental model of a large, unfamiliar codebase before making changes.
stem: What is the best strategy for building understanding of a large, unfamiliar codebase?

options.text: Read all files upfront to load complete context before answering questions.
Start with Grep to find entry points, then use Read to follow imports and trace flows incrementally.
Ask the agent to summarize the codebase from typical patterns for that kind of project.
Glob every file and Read them in alphabetical order.

rationale.correct: Incremental exploration — Grep for entry points, then Read to follow imports and trace flows — builds accurate understanding without exhausting the context window.

distractors.A: Reading everything upfront wastes context and dilutes attention across mostly-irrelevant files.
distractors.C: Relying on ‘typical patterns’ for the project type invents details instead of reading the actual code.
distractors.D: Reading every file in alphabetical order has the same context-exhaustion problem as reading everything upfront, without even prioritizing relevance.

scenario: Ten minutes into a brand-new session with almost no prior exploration yet, an agent answers a question about a specific class by describing 'typical patterns for this kind of service' instead of the actual class.
stem: Is this the same context-degradation signature described elsewhere, and does a scratchpad file fix it?

options.text: Yes to both — any 'typical patterns' phrasing is context degradation by definition, and a scratchpad always resolves it.

No — with almost no session history yet, there's little context to have degraded; the more likely cause is that the agent hasn't actually explored the specific class yet, so grep/read the actual code first rather than reaching for a scratchpad.
Yes, but the fix is different — restart the session entirely rather than using a scratchpad.
No — this indicates the model is fundamentally incapable of understanding the codebase, regardless of session length.

rationale.correct: Context degradation describes specific findings getting diluted or pushed out over a long session; ten minutes into a fresh session with minimal history, there isn't much to have degraded. Falling back to general patterns this early more likely means the code hasn't actually been read yet — the fix is incremental exploration (grep then read), not a scratchpad meant for a different problem.

distractors.A: The phrasing alone doesn't establish the cause; session length and prior investigation depth matter, and both are minimal here.
distractors.C: Restarting a session that's already only ten minutes old addresses nothing, since there's little accumulated context to lose either way.
distractors.D: A capability conclusion isn't supported by an agent simply not yet having explored a specific file it hasn't been directed to yet.

scenario: You're deep into exploring a large codebase and your context window is filling with useful discovery output. You're deciding between running `/compact` now versus ending the session and starting fresh with an injected summary of key findings.
stem: What should determine which approach you take?

options.text: Whether you want to keep working within the same session's flow (favor `/compact`, which condenses in place but is lossy) versus whether a clean, deliberately-curated restart would better preserve exactly the findings that matter (favor a fresh session with an explicit summary, especially if some of the accumulated context is no longer relevant or has become noisy).
Always use `/compact`, since it is strictly better than starting a new session in every situation.
Always start a fresh session, since compaction is never useful.
The choice makes no difference; both approaches produce identical results.

rationale.correct: The two tools solve overlapping but distinct problems: `/compact` condenses in place with some information loss, useful for continuing the same flow; starting fresh with an explicit, curated summary lets you deliberately choose what to carry forward and drop accumulated noise or staleness — which one fits better depends on the situation.

distractors.B: `/compact` is lossy and doesn't offer the deliberate curation a fresh, explicit summary can — it isn't strictly better in every case.
distractors.C: `/compact` is a real, useful tool for continuing within a session without losing the current flow; dismissing it entirely ignores a legitimate option.
distractors.D: The two approaches have different tradeoffs (lossy in-place condensation vs. a deliberately curated restart) and can produce meaningfully different outcomes.

scenario: Before starting a large codebase exploration, you have a fixed overall context budget for the whole task: exploration plus the actual work that follows it. You haven't set any limit on how much of that budget exploration itself may consume.
stem: What is the risk of not budgeting exploration separately, and the better approach?

options.text: Unbounded exploration can consume most or all of the available context before any actual work begins, leaving little room to act on what was learned; deliberately reserving a portion of the budget for the actual task (and using techniques like scratchpads or subagent delegation to keep exploration itself efficient) avoids that outcome.
There is no risk; exploration and the actual task always divide the available context evenly on their own.
The only fix is to skip exploration entirely and start acting on the codebase with no investigation.
Budgeting doesn't matter, since context degradation only happens near the very end of a session regardless of how it was used earlier.

rationale.correct: Without an explicit reservation, exploration can consume the lion's share of the available context before the actual task even starts, since nothing is automatically balancing the two; consciously allocating budget (and using efficient exploration techniques) protects room for the work exploration was meant to inform.

distractors.B: Context isn't automatically balanced between exploration and later work; an unbounded exploration phase can consume a disproportionate share.
distractors.C: Skipping exploration entirely trades one problem (context exhaustion) for another (acting on the codebase without understanding it).
distractors.D: Context degradation and exhaustion risk build up based on how much has been consumed already, not strictly on session position; spending too much early still leaves too little for later.

scenario: A team is ready to segment their 97%-aggregate extraction accuracy figure but is unsure which breakdowns are worth computing first, given limited analysis time.
stem: Which breakdowns are most likely to reveal a masked problem, and why?

options.text: Only a breakdown by the day of the week the document was processed, since accuracy could plausibly vary by processing schedule.

Breakdowns by document type and by individual field, since aggregate accuracy is a volume-weighted average that can hide a minority document type or a specific field performing far worse than the overall number suggests.
Only a breakdown by which team member configured the extraction pipeline, since human factors are the most likely hidden variable.
No breakdown is more informative than another; any single cut is equally likely to reveal a problem.

rationale.correct: Document type and field are the dimensions where a volume-weighted aggregate is most likely to mask trouble: a low-volume document type or a specific field can perform far worse than the aggregate suggests while barely moving the overall number. Processing day or configurer identity aren't the mechanisms this masking effect actually depends on.

distractors.A: Day-of-week isn't the dimension the volume-weighting masking effect operates on; it's a plausible but much lower-value first cut than type/field.
distractors.C: Configurer identity isn't established as a relevant factor here and isn't where the volume-weighting effect hides problems.
distractors.D: Not all cuts are equally informative; type and field are specifically where a volume-weighted aggregate is known to mask segment-level problems.

scenario: A team wants to calibrate field-level confidence scores against labeled data to drive review routing, but only has 200 labeled examples so far, far fewer than they'd like.
stem: What is the most reasonable way to proceed given the limited labeled set?

options.text: Skip calibration entirely and route based on raw model-reported confidence until a much larger labeled set exists.

Use the 200 examples for an initial calibration, treat it as provisional, and expand the labeled set over time (e.g., by continuing to sample and label extractions) to refine the calibration as more data accumulates.
Wait until a labeled set of at least several thousand examples exists before doing any calibration work at all.
Use the 200 examples to calibrate once, and never revisit the calibration regardless of how much more labeled data becomes available later.

rationale.correct: An initial, provisional calibration from the available data is more useful than none, as long as it's treated as a starting point to refine as the labeled set grows — this avoids both the unreliability of uncalibrated raw confidence and an indefinite wait for a large labeled set before doing anything.

distractors.A: Uncalibrated raw confidence is exactly the unreliable signal calibration is meant to fix; using it by default while waiting isn't the better option.
distractors.C: Waiting for a large labeled set before any calibration work defers a usable improvement for no clear benefit over a provisional, refinable calibration.
distractors.D: Treating an early calibration as permanent ignores that more labeled data becoming available is a reason to refine it, not a fact to ignore.

scenario: For six months, human reviewers have been correcting a meaningful share of low-confidence extractions, but those corrections are only ever used to approve the individual document in front of the reviewer — the underlying extraction prompt has never been updated based on what reviewers keep fixing.
stem: What is the missed opportunity here, and the fix?

options.text: Reviewer corrections are a rich signal for improving the extraction prompt itself (e.g., patterns in what's commonly miscorrected can point to specific prompt gaps); periodically analyzing correction patterns and feeding them back into prompt refinement closes the loop, rather than only ever fixing one document at a time.
Nothing is missing — using corrections solely to approve individual documents is the entire intended purpose of human review.
The fix is to stop using human review entirely, since it isn't improving the model on its own.
Reviewer corrections should be discarded once a document is approved, since they have no further value.

rationale.correct: Review corrections carry systematic information about where the extraction is weak — recurring correction patterns are exactly the kind of signal that should feed back into refining the prompt (new examples, tightened criteria, schema tweaks), not just fix one document at a time forever with the same underlying gaps.

distractors.B: Human review can serve both purposes — approving individual documents now, and improving the system going forward — and only using it for the former leaves real, available improvement on the table.
distractors.C: Review itself is working (documents are getting corrected); the missed opportunity is using its output more fully, not eliminating it.
distractors.D: Discarding correction data after approval throws away exactly the signal that could reduce how often review is needed in the first place.

scenario: Two human reviewers independently check the same sample of extractions as part of a calibration exercise. On 15% of documents, they disagree with each other about whether the model's extraction was correct.
stem: What does this level of reviewer disagreement imply for the calibration effort?

options.text: The 'ground truth' labels themselves have real uncertainty where reviewers disagree; that uncertainty limits how precisely you can calibrate model confidence against those labels, and resolving reviewer disagreements (e.g., via a clear adjudication rule or a third reviewer) improves the quality of the labeled set the calibration depends on.
Reviewer disagreement is irrelevant to calibration, since only the model's confidence score matters.
The 15% disagreement rate should be added directly to the model's reported accuracy figure without further analysis.
Human review should be abandoned in favor of trusting the model's self-reported confidence exclusively, since humans clearly aren't reliable either.

rationale.correct: Calibrating model confidence against human labels assumes those labels are a solid ground truth; when reviewers themselves disagree at a meaningful rate, that assumption weakens, and the calibration is only as good as the labeled set — improving reviewer agreement (via clearer guidelines or adjudication) strengthens the foundation the whole calibration effort rests on.

distractors.B: The labels calibration is checked against matter directly; unreliable ground truth undermines how much you can trust the resulting calibration.
distractors.C: Disagreement rate and accuracy are different measurements; conflating them doesn't correctly characterize either the model's performance or the labels' reliability.
distractors.D: Reviewer disagreement is a signal to improve the human labeling process, not a reason to abandon human review and rely solely on the model's own, uncalibrated self-assessment.

scenario: A research system's claim-source mappings correctly preserve attribution through synthesis. Weeks later, one cited source is discovered to have been retracted by its publisher after the report was generated.
stem: What does the existing claim-source mapping design let the team do that a report without structured attribution would not?

options.text: Nothing additional; structured attribution only helps at synthesis time, not after a report has already shipped.

Precisely identify every claim in the shipped report that depended on the retracted source, so those specific claims (and only those) can be flagged or revisited, rather than needing to re-examine the entire report.
Automatically and silently correct the retracted claims without any human review.
Prevent the source from ever having been retracted in the first place.

rationale.correct: Because each claim is explicitly tied to its source, a later problem with one source (like a retraction) can be traced to exactly the claims that depended on it — a targeted, traceable follow-up that a report without structured attribution couldn't support without re-reviewing everything from scratch.

distractors.A: The traceability structured attribution provides doesn't expire at synthesis time; it's exactly what makes a later audit like this possible.
distractors.C: Structured attribution supports identifying affected claims; it doesn't itself make a correctness judgment or replace human review of what to do about them.
distractors.D: Attribution structure has no bearing on whether an external publisher retracts a source; it only affects how traceable the consequences are.

scenario: Three credible sources report a metric: two report figures within 2% of each other, and a third reports a figure 40% higher than the other two.
stem: Does the two-source agreement change how the synthesis agent should handle the outlier, compared to a simple two-source disagreement?

options.text: Yes — with two sources agreeing, the synthesis agent should simply drop the outlier and report only the agreed-upon figure as if no conflict existed.

No in substance — the agent should still present all three figures with attribution and annotate the discrepancy, though it can note that two of the three are mutually consistent as part of that annotation, rather than silently discarding the outlier.
Yes — majority agreement among sources is sufficient grounds to treat the third source as definitively wrong and exclude it from the report entirely.
No — the agent should average all three figures into a single blended number to resolve the conflict.

rationale.correct: Two sources agreeing doesn't establish that the third is factually wrong — it could reflect a different methodology or timeframe. The agent should still preserve all three with attribution, annotating that two are mutually consistent as useful context, rather than silently dropping or definitively excluding the outlier.

distractors.A: Dropping the outlier silently discards information the reader may need, exactly as a two-source disagreement would.
distractors.C: Numeric agreement among sources isn't proof of correctness; the third source may reflect a legitimate methodological or temporal difference not yet understood.
distractors.D: Averaging in a third figure produces a number none of the three sources actually reported and still hides the underlying disagreement.

scenario: Subagent outputs already include collection dates in their structured fields. Despite this, a synthesis report still flags two same-metric figures from 2022 and 2024 as 'contradictory' without noting the year difference.
stem: Given that dates are already captured, what is the correct next fix?

options.text: Add dates to the structured output, since that is always the fix for this class of problem.

Explicitly instruct the synthesis step to compare available date/collection metadata before labeling any two figures as contradictory, since the dates being present in the data doesn't guarantee the synthesis reasoning step actually uses them.
Remove all older data from consideration, since only the most recent figure should ever be reported.
Add a conflict_detected boolean field, since that will resolve the misclassification on its own.

rationale.correct: The dates are already captured, so the gap has moved downstream: the synthesis step isn't using the metadata it has. The fix is to explicitly direct synthesis to check temporal metadata before calling two figures contradictory — capturing the data was necessary but not, on its own, sufficient.

distractors.A: Dates are already present in this scenario; re-adding data that already exists doesn't address why synthesis isn't using it.
distractors.C: Discarding older data throws away legitimate historical figures and doesn't address the actual reasoning gap.
distractors.D: A boolean flag doesn't supply reasoning about temporal context; it's a label, not the comparison the synthesis step still needs to perform.

scenario: A synthesis agent combines three subagent findings, each individually well-sourced but each only weakly suggestive on its own, to arrive at an overall conclusion ('the market is likely shifting toward subscription models'). No individual source states this conclusion directly — it's an inference the synthesis agent is drawing by connecting the three findings.
stem: How should the synthesis output represent this conclusion?

options.text: Explicitly flag it as a synthesized inference (not something any single source directly stated), citing the three supporting findings, and characterize it with appropriate uncertainty rather than presenting it with the same confidence as a directly-sourced fact.
State the conclusion as a plain, directly-sourced fact, since it's supported by three real findings.
Omit the conclusion entirely, since no single source states it outright.
Attribute the conclusion to whichever one of the three sources seems most authoritative, as if that source stated it alone.

rationale.correct: An inference drawn by combining multiple partial findings is a different kind of claim than something a source states directly — it should be labeled as synthesized reasoning, backed by its supporting findings, and given uncertainty appropriate to an inference rather than the confidence of a directly-cited fact.

distractors.B: Presenting an inferred conclusion with the same confidence as a directly-stated fact overstates what the sources actually established individually.
distractors.C: A well-supported inference is valuable information; omitting it discards a genuine synthesis insight rather than just correctly characterizing its nature.
distractors.D: Attributing a conclusion no single source actually stated to just one of them misrepresents where the conclusion actually came from.
